X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Biesse Hobbyist Machines
X1.method: Online survey with a controlled choice experiment. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual woodworkers and hobbyists. Each participant views a product description of a Biesse desktop CNC machine and is presented with two price points: a premium price (e.g., €3,000) and a standard hobbyist price (e.g., €1,500). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase the machine at each price point and to state their primary reason for choosing the machine.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 200 participants (100 per price point) from a panel of individual woodworkers and hobbyists in the United States and Europe. Recruitment via online panels and social media groups.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the machine at the premium price. Secondary outcomes: proportion of participants who choose the premium price over the standard price, and self-reported primary purchase reason (precision/quality vs. community).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants will choose the premium price, and the premium price will be selected by a majority of respondents.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% of participants will choose the premium price, but the premium price will be selected by fewer respondents than the standard price, and community reasons will be cited by a majority of premium-price buyers.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium-price choice rate is at least 30% across both price points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the premium-price choice rate is below 30% or the standard-price choice rate is significantly higher, consider no expansion or a different value proposition. If the premium-price choice rate is between 20% and 30%, conduct a follow-up survey to validate the premium-price preference before committing to a full consumer launch.

final.recommendation: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (X1) to test whether individual woodworkers and hobbyists are willing to pay a premium price for Biesse machines. If the premium-price choice rate is at least 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops. If the rate is below 30%, consider no expansion or a different value proposition before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Individual woodworkers and hobbyists who value precision, quality, and professional-grade performance, and are willing to invest in machines that meet industrial standards.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Biesse machines as premium, high-performance tools for hobbyists and small workshops, leveraging the company's reputation for quality and precision to justify premium pricing.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (X1) with a sample of 200 participants, analyze results, and decide on a go/no-go basis for a consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market, willingness to pay a premium price, and the competitive landscape for consumer-grade CNC machines are uncertain. The survey results will be the primary source of evidence.
would_change_if: If the premium-price choice rate is below 30% or the standard-price choice rate is significantly higher, indicating limited demand for a premium proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for community and collaboration features, which would shift the value proposition toward a community-driven model.

X1.name: Premium vs Eco-Friendly Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual woodworkers and hobbyists. Each participant views a product description of a Biesse desktop CNC machine with either premium positioning (emphasizing industrial precision and professional-grade quality) or eco-friendly positioning (emphasizing sustainability, eco-certifications, and environmental responsibility). They are then asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and whether they would purchase the machine.
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.
X1.measure: 1) Average maximum price willingness to pay (EUR). 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Share of participants indicating they would buy each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average maximum price and higher purchase intent for the premium condition compared to the eco-friendly condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average maximum price and higher purchase intent for the eco-friendly condition compared to the premium condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium condition's average maximum price is at least 20% higher than the eco-friendly condition's average maximum price, and the premium condition's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the eco-friendly condition's purchase intent, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition based on premium positioning. If the premium condition's average maximum price is at least 20% higher and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 percentage points, recommend a premium-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets the thresholds, recommend no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Biesse S.p.A. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.

frame.objective: Determine whether Brembo N.V. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current brake systems and aftermarket replacement parts, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., performance brake kits for hobbyists, racing enthusiasts, or custom builds).
2) Expand the aftermarket by offering premium replacement parts or service contracts for individual consumers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B brake systems and aftermarket parts without new consumer offerings.
4) Partner with existing consumer brands to co‑brand brake components for individual buyers (e.g., limited‑edition disc kits).
5) Target a new consumer segment such as electric vehicle (EV) owners with specialized brake systems.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test for Performance Brake Kit
X1.method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign with two versions: Version A (performance-focused) and Version B (lifestyle-focused). Both ads feature a Brembo brake kit at a premium price (e.g., €1,200). Version A emphasizes heritage, performance, and sporty aesthetics; Version B emphasizes lifestyle, status, and the Brembo lifestyle collection. Track clicks, conversions, and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: Estimated 5,000 individual buyers in the UK and Germany who have shown interest in performance upgrades (e.g., visited a performance car forum or purchased an upgrade kit in the past 12 months).
X1.measure: Conversion rate (percentage of visitors who click the buy button) and average willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Version A will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version B, because performance-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to performance messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Version B will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version A, because lifestyle-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to status and brand messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If Version A conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition. If Version B conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer offerings.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed digital messaging test (X1) to empirically compare performance and lifestyle messaging. If Version A meets the conversion and willingness-to-pay thresholds, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition; if Version B meets thresholds, proceed with a lifestyle-focused proposition. If neither meets thresholds, do not expand into consumer offerings at this time.
final.target_customer: Performance-oriented individual buyers (e.g., track day enthusiasts, racing enthusiasts, and high-performance car owners) who value superior braking performance and a sporty aesthetic.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated brake kit that combines Brembo's heritage, performance heritage, and market-leading adjustability, sold at a premium price through Brembo's lifestyle collection and e-commerce platform.
final.next_action: Execute the digital messaging test (X1) within the 12-week timeline and 20,000 EUR budget, analyzing conversion rates and willingness to pay to decide whether to pursue a performance-focused or lifestyle-focused consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the target segment of individual buyers, their willingness to pay a premium price, and the competitive landscape for performance brake kits are uncertain. The test will provide empirical evidence to resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows Version A (performance-focused) achieving a conversion rate of at least 5% and an average willingness to pay of at least €1,200, the recommendation would shift to proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition.

If the test shows Version B (lifestyle-focused) achieving a conversion rate of at least 5% and an average willingness to pay of at least €1,200, the recommendation would shift to proceed with a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition.
If neither version meets the thresholds, the recommendation would remain to not expand into consumer offerings at this time.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider Rieter’s existing B2B focus and its ownership of Barmag.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists or small-scale producers (e.g., compact spinning kits, DIY spinning machines).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new industrial features or services to existing short-staple spinning machines.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial spinning mills and after‑sales services.
4) License Barmag technology to third‑party consumer brands for spinning equipment.

T1.claim: Individual crafters and hobbyists purchase spinning equipment primarily for the satisfaction of making yarn and the creative process, not for profit or mass production. If Rieter offers a differentiated consumer proposition, they will buy it because they already use or admire Rieter machines and want to keep the craft personal.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists and small-scale crafters who value the creative experience of spinning.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Their purchase decision is driven by personal enjoyment, not by a need for large-scale production capacity.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter can sell premium-priced, differentiated kits or machines directly to consumers at a margin, leveraging its brand reputation and design.
assumptions: Consumers already own or admire Rieter machines.
They are willing to pay a premium for a differentiated offering.
The market for individual spinning is large enough to support a consumer line.
predictions: Consumers will express willingness to pay above the price of standard industrial machines.
Purchases will be motivated by personal enjoyment rather than production scale.
Sales will be concentrated among hobbyists and small-scale producers rather than large-scale mills.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Personal Enjoyment vs Functional Need
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A (personal enjoyment) and Group B (functional need). Each group views a product description of a Rieter-inspired spinning machine and is asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 per group, recruited via craft and hobby forums to ensure self-identified crafters and small-scale producers.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑2 scale) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, indicating purchase driven by personal enjoyment.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, indicating purchase driven by functional need.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group B’s, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on personal enjoyment. If Group B’s average WTP is at least 20% higher, develop a proposition focused on functional capacity. If the difference is less than 20%, no expansion is recommended.

final.target_customer: Hobbyists and small-scale crafters who value the creative experience of spinning.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated, affordable spinning kit or machine that emphasizes personal enjoyment, brand reputation, and ease of use, leveraging Rieter’s existing artisan line.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (choice-based conjoint) to distinguish between personal enjoyment and functional need motivations before committing to a consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The evidence does not confirm whether consumers already own Rieter machines, are motivated by personal enjoyment, or are driven by functional needs. Financial constraints limit the test budget to €20,000 and the timeframe to 12 weeks.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B’s average willingness to pay is at least 20% higher than Group A’s, indicating functional need drives purchases.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider Rieter’s existing B2B focus and its ownership of Barmag.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists or small-scale producers (e.g., compact spinning kits, DIY spinning machines).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new industrial features or services to existing short-staple spinning machines.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial spinning mills and after‑sales services.
4) License Barmag technology to third‑party consumer brands for spinning equipment.

T1.claim: Hobbyists and small-scale producers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need affordable, compact spinning equipment to create handmade yarn, and Rieter can capture value by selling integrated machines and accessories directly to them.
T1.who_benefits: Hobbyists and small-scale producers gain easy-to-use spinning equipment; Rieter gains higher-margin direct sales and brand exposure.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They currently lack access to compact, affordable spinning machines; a consumer proposition removes this barrier and makes spinning accessible.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells machines and accessories through its webshop, earning revenue per unit and potentially higher margins than B2B sales.

X1.name: Hobbyist Willingness-to-Pay Survey
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from a panel of hobbyists and small-scale producers. They are shown a mock product description of a compact spinning machine (e.g., a mini card spinning machine) and asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the features they would accept. The survey also includes a willingness-to-pay question for a premium version with additional features.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 300 participants (150 hobbyists and 150 small-scale producers) recruited via an online panel. Stratified by age, gender, and geographic region to ensure diversity.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the compact spinning machine. Secondary measure: share of participants who would pay a premium over a baseline price of CHF 200.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP will be above CHF 200, and at least 30% of participants will indicate a premium price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP will be below CHF 200, and fewer than 20% of participants will indicate a premium price.

X1.decision_rule: If average WTP is above CHF 200 and at least 30% indicate a premium price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average WTP is below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, do not invest in a consumer proposition. If the average WTP is between CHF 150 and CHF 200, conduct a follow-up survey to understand the reasons for the lower price sensitivity.

final.recommendation: Proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small-scale producers, as supported by the Artisan line and the presence of a consumer webshop. However, validate demand through a willingness-to-pay survey before committing resources. If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and low premium pricing, reconsider the investment; otherwise, develop a compact spinning machine,
final.target_customer: Hobbyists and small-scale producers who currently lack access to compact, affordable spinning equipment.
final.value_proposition: An affordable, compact spinning machine that automates key steps and brings speed to the creative process, sold through Rieter’s existing webshop.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €15,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 300 participants to measure price sensitivity and premium willingness. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development or abandon the consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The actual size of the hobbyist market and Rieter’s ability to produce a profitable consumer product remain uncertain. Financial constraints (e.g., net loss in 2025) and the lack of public evidence on willingness to pay add to the ambiguity
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, reconsider the investment.

If new evidence shows a large, growing market for home spinning or Rieter’s ability to achieve positive margins on a consumer product, the recommendation would shift toward developing the proposition.

arguments.name: Hobbyist Willingness-to-Pay Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from a panel of hobbyists and small-scale producers. They are shown a mock product description of a compact spinning machine (e.g., a mini card spinning machine) and asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the features they would accept. The survey also includes a willingness-to-pay question for a premium version with additional features.
arguments.sample: Proposed sample: 300 participants (150 hobbyists and 150 small-scale producers) recruited via an online panel. Stratified by age, gender, and geographic region to ensure diversity.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the compact spinning machine. Secondary measure: share of participants who would pay a premium over a baseline price of CHF 200.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average WTP will be above CHF 200, and at least 30% of participants will indicate a premium price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average WTP will be below CHF 200, and fewer than 20% of participants will indicate a premium price.

arguments.decision_rule: If average WTP is above CHF 200 and at least 30% indicate a premium price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average WTP is below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, do not invest in a consumer proposition. If the average WTP is between CHF 150 and CHF 200, conduct a follow-up survey to understand the reasons for the lower price sensitivity.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small-scale producers, as supported by the Artisan line and the presence of a consumer webshop. However, validate demand through a willingness-to-pay survey before committing resources. If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and low premium pricing, reconsider the investment; otherwise, develop a compact spinning machine,

arguments.target_customer: Hobbyists and small-scale producers who currently lack access to compact, affordable spinning equipment.
arguments.value_proposition: An affordable, compact spinning machine that automates key steps and brings speed to the creative process, sold through Rieter’s existing webshop.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €15,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 300 participants to measure price sensitivity and premium willingness. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development or abandon the consumer proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: The actual size of the hobbyist market and Rieter’s ability to produce a profitable consumer product remain uncertain. Financial constraints (e.g., net loss in 2025) and the lack of public evidence on willingness to pay add to the ambiguity
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, reconsider the investment.

X1.name: Consumer vs Industrial Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing reduced manual labor and higher yield for hobbyists. Group B sees an industrial-focused message emphasizing scalability and modularity for small-scale producers. Both groups are presented with a product description of a compact spinning machine priced at €1,500 (T1) or €3,000 (T2). Participants indicate their likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (self-identified crafters) and 250 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely"). Secondary measure: stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, indicating demand for a consumer proposition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, indicating demand for an industrial proposition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A and the difference is statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

frame.objective: Determine whether Sika AG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify such investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Need to assess current consumer reach and demand for Sika products.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.
Any recommendation must consider Sika’s existing B2B business and potential disruption to current revenue streams.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., DIY waterproofing for residential homeowners).
2) Expand the B2B portfolio by adding new industrial or automotive applications without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B markets (contractors, distributors, manufacturers).
4) Change the route to market for existing B2B products to reach individual buyers directly (e.g., e‑commerce, direct‑to‑consumer sales).
5) Target a different customer group within the B2B space (e.g., small‑to‑medium residential contractors) with a differentiated offering.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners see Sika products used by professionals and hear about their performance, they will shift from generic or cheaper alternatives to a trusted brand, increasing purchase frequency.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika can capture value through premium pricing, brand positioning as a professional-grade brand, and potentially through distribution channels that already serve contractors and DIYers.
assumptions: Homeowners are aware of professional-grade sealants and can distinguish them from consumer-grade products.
Professional contractors continue to recommend Sika products to homeowners.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality and reliability.
predictions: Homeowners will purchase Sika sealants at a higher price point than generic alternatives when presented with professional endorsements.
Purchase intent will be higher among homeowners who have worked with professional contractors.

X1.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional Grade vs Convenience Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Grade (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and durability) or Convenience (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). Both conditions present a product description of a Sika sealant for a specific use case (e.g., waterproofing a basement). Participants are asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the maximum price they would pay. X1.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

arguments.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.
arguments.sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider TOMRA’s existing B2B customers and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition targeting individual households (e.g., home recycling for single‑use containers).
2) Expand B2B offerings by targeting new segments such as small retailers, food processors, or mining companies with additional sorting or recycling solutions.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets without new consumer initiatives.
4) License TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting technology to third‑party consumer brands for integrated recycling solutions.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive a clear, direct financial benefit (deposit refunds) and a convenient digital experience, because they value immediate financial reward and simplicity over traditional collection methods.
T1.who_benefits: Households with single-use containers who currently drop off containers at bag-drops or redemption centers.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are motivated by the tangible return of their deposit and the convenience of a digital app, which reduces the effort of finding a collection point and waiting for a refund.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through a subscription or transaction fee for the digital payout service, plus potential data monetization from recycling behavior insights.
assumptions: Consumers currently use bag-drops or redemption centers for deposit returns.
A digital payout system can be integrated without major retailer infrastructure changes.
Consumers are willing to pay a small fee for the digital service.
predictions: In a test offering a digital payout app with a refund threshold of €5, at least 30% of targeted households will complete a deposit return transaction within 12 weeks.
User retention rate for the app will be above 20% after 12 weeks, indicating continued usage beyond the initial refund.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are motivated by the belief that their individual actions contribute to a larger environmental goal, creating a sense of purpose and community involvement.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through a subscription or participation fee that funds environmental initiatives, plus potential brand association with sustainability.
assumptions: Consumers currently recycle but lack a mechanism to track their impact.
A community-driven platform can be built without requiring retailer or government involvement.
Consumers are willing to pay a fee for the environmental impact tracking service.
predictions: In a test offering a community impact tracking app with a participation fee of €2 per month, at least 25% of targeted households will sign up within 12 weeks.

X1.name: Digital Payout vs Environmental Tracking Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a digital payout app (financial reward) or an environmental impact tracking app (community-driven). Participants are recruited from households with single-use containers. Each arm offers a refund or participation fee, and a follow-up survey measures intent to adopt and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 500 households (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and recycling frequency.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: percentage of households choosing the arm (digital payout vs environmental tracking) within 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay (refund amount) and intent to adopt (binary).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Digital payout arm will achieve at least 30% choice rate and higher willingness to pay than environmental tracking arm.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Environmental tracking arm will achieve at least 25% choice rate and higher willingness to pay than digital payout arm.

X1.decision_rule: If digital payout arm choice rate ≥ 30% and its willingness to pay ≥ €5, proceed to develop a digital payout consumer proposition. If environmental tracking arm choice rate ≥ 25% and its willingness to pay ≥ €2, develop an environmental impact tracking proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

final.recommendation: Proceed to develop a digital payout consumer proposition for individual households, as it is supported by evidence of TOMRA’s existing consumer app (myTOMRA) and the popularity of bag-drops. The test should measure choice rate and willingness to pay to validate demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: Households with single-use containers who currently use bag-drops or redemption centers for deposit returns.
final.value_proposition: A digital payout app that provides immediate deposit refunds and a map to nearby recycling points, making recycling more convenient and financially rewarding.

final.uncertainty: The evidence does not show whether consumers are motivated by financial reward or environmental responsibility, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for a digital payout service. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the environmental tracking arm achieving at least 25% choice rate and a willingness to pay of €2 per month, we would reconsider a community-driven proposition.
If the test fails to meet the choice rate or refund threshold, we would abandon expansion and focus on existing B2B markets.

X1.name: Homeowner Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners in target regions (e.g., Germany, Austria, Switzerland) who own a motorhome, RV, or car with auxiliary heaters.
X1.measure: Average WTP in euros for a home unit compared to a standard 12V heater, and self-reported primary motivation (safety/comfort vs. weight/fuel efficiency).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the home unit than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be safety/comfort.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the home unit that emphasizes weight savings/fuel efficiency than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be performance.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the home unit exceeds the WTP for the 12V heater by at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated parking-heater offer test (SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE) does not provide evidence that homeowners are aware of Eberspacher or willing to pay a premium for home units; it only tests installation friction. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on safety and comfort benefits. Begin with a targeted online survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate willingness to pay and primary motivation before committing to product development.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who own motorhomes, RVs, or car auxiliary heaters in regions with extreme weather conditions where vehicle auxiliary heaters are insufficient.
final.value_proposition: A dedicated Eberspacher home unit that delivers reliable, consistent heating performance and safety, addressing the gap left by vehicle auxiliary heaters.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Homeowner Preference Test (500 homeowners, €15,000, 8 weeks) to measure willingness to pay and primary motivation before any product development.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether homeowners are aware of Eberspacher and willing to pay a premium for home units. If the test shows a willingness-to-pay gap of less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, the investment
would_change_if: The test shows a willingness-to-pay gap of at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, indicating strong consumer demand for a differentiated home unit.
Evidence emerges that homeowners are aware of Eberspacher and actively seek premium-priced home units, supporting T2.

arguments.name: Homeowner Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners in target regions (e.g., Germany, Austria, Switzerland) who own a motorhome, RV, or car with auxiliary heaters.
arguments.measure: Average WTP in euros for a home unit compared to a standard 12V heater, and self-reported primary motivation (safety/comfort vs. weight/fuel efficiency).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average WTP for the home unit than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be safety/comfort.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average WTP for the home unit that emphasizes weight savings/fuel efficiency than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be performance.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the home unit exceeds the WTP for the 12V heater by at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Premium vs. Safety‑Critical Home Heating Kit Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in cold climates. They are shown two identical product descriptions for a premium‑priced home heating kit, differing only in the highlighted benefit: (A) premium safety and reliability (e.g., "proven automotive safety, reliable heating for extreme cold") or (B) safety‑critical, fuel‑independent (e.g., "no gas bottles, permanent heating, weight savings"). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and state their top reason for choosing the kit.
X1.sample: 400 homeowners in cold climates (e.g., northern Germany, UK, US) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and heating‑current‑use status.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and the top reason stated by participants.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and stated reason of premium safety and reliability when the benefit is highlighted as "premium safety and reliability."
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and stated reason of safety‑critical, fuel‑independent when the benefit is highlighted as "safety‑critical, fuel‑independent."

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the premium‑safety message is at least 1.5 points higher than for the safety‑critical message, conclude T1 is more supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is significantly supported. If both messages show similar intent, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.

It tests installation friction, not consumer preference for premium safety. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, price sensitivity, and competitive landscape are uncertain. The test will clarify whether there is sufficient demand to justify investment in a differentiated consumer proposition.

arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in cold climates. They are shown two identical product descriptions for a premium‑priced home heating kit, differing only in the highlighted benefit: (A) premium safety and reliability (e.g., "proven automotive safety, reliable heating for extreme cold") or (B) safety‑critical, fuel‑independent (e.g., "no gas bottles, permanent heating, weight savings"). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and state their top reason for choosing the kit.
arguments.sample: 400 homeowners in cold climates (e.g., northern Germany, UK, US) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and heating‑current‑use status.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested) and the top reason stated by participants.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for the premium‑safety message is at least 1.5 points higher than for the safety‑critical message, conclude T1 is more supported. result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Homeowners vs High-End RV Owners
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowners group (n=300) or a high‑end RV group (n=300). Each group sees a product description of an integrated thermal management kit for RVs/motorhomes, priced 20% above a generic equivalent. Homeowners are asked to state primary purchase reasons (comfort, safety, convenience, brand). High‑end RV owners are asked the same, plus willingness to pay a premium. A decision rule: if homeowners report comfort/safety as primary reason and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners report performance/brand premium and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, the theory is not supported.
X1.sample: 300 homeowners and 300 high‑end RV owners, recruited via an online panel to match demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary purchase reason (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (binary: would pay more).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will report comfort/safety as primary reason and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: High‑end RV owners will report performance/brand premium and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowners meet the comfort/safety threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners meet the performance/brand threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, neither theory is supported.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Homeowners vs High-End RV Owners
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowners group (n=300) or a high‑end RV group (n=300). Each group sees a product description of an integrated thermal management kit for RVs/motorhomes, priced 20% above a generic equivalent. Homeowners are asked to state primary purchase reasons (comfort, safety, convenience, brand). High‑end RV owners are asked the same, plus willingness to pay a premium. A decision rule: if homeowners report comfort/safety as primary reason and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners report performance/brand premium and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, the theory is not supported.
arguments.sample: 300 homeowners and 300 high‑end RV owners, recruited via an online panel to match demographics.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary purchase reason (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (binary: would pay more).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will report comfort/safety as primary reason and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: High‑end RV owners will report performance/brand premium and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.

arguments.decision_rule: If homeowners meet the comfort/safety threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners meet the performance/brand threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, neither theory is supported.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated parking-heater offer test (SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE) does not provide evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or brand recognition among homeowners. It tests installation friction, not purchase intent. Therefore it does not affect T1.

tool_result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial precision rotary cutting tools.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists, DIY enthusiasts, or small‑to‑medium manufacturers for a specific use case (e.g., home woodworkers, small metal fabrication).

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hobbyist Tools
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and small‑to‑medium manufacturers. They view a product description of a Gühring precision rotary tool and are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the likelihood they would purchase it. The survey also asks about current tool sources and preference for a single‑source toolkit.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 hobbyists (home woodworkers) and 150 small‑to‑medium manufacturers. Recruitment via hobbyist forums, trade associations, and industry groups.
X1.measure: 1) Maximum price willingness to pay (WTP) for Gühring vs generic alternatives. 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Preference for a single‑source toolkit (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show WTP at least 20% higher for Gühring than for generic alternatives, and purchase intent will be high (>=60%).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Hobbyists will show WTP at least 15% higher for a single‑source Gühring kit than for a multi‑vendor kit, and purchase intent will be high (>=60%).

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Gühring among hobbyists is >=20% above the WTP for generic alternatives and >=15% above the WTP for a single‑source kit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is <10% for hobbyists or <5% for manufacturers, consider no expansion. If neither condition is met, conduct further market research.

arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hobbyist Tools
arguments.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and small‑to‑medium manufacturers. They view a product description of a Gühring precision rotary tool and are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the likelihood they would purchase it. The survey also asks about current tool sources and preference for a single‑source toolkit.
arguments.sample: 300 respondents: 150 hobbyists (home woodworkers) and 150 small‑to‑medium manufacturers. Recruitment via hobbyist forums, trade associations, and industry groups.
arguments.measure: 1) Maximum price willingness to pay (WTP) for Gühring vs generic alternatives. 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Preference for a single‑source toolkit (yes/no).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show WTP at least 20% higher for Gühring than for generic alternatives, and purchase intent will be high (>=60%).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Hobbyists will show WTP at least 15% higher for a single‑source Gühring kit than for a multi‑vendor kit, and purchase intent will be high (>=60%).

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Gühring among hobbyists is >=20% above the WTP for generic alternatives and >=15% above the WTP for a single‑source kit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is <10% for hobbyists or <5% for manufacturers, consider no expansion. If neither condition is met, conduct further market research.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign within Gühring’s existing B2B digital shop, offering a differentiated consumer‑focused precision rotary tool for a specific use case (e.g., home woodwork). The ad will present two versions: Version A emphasizes premium quality and precision (e.g., "Top‑notch precision for professional results"), and Version B emphasizes convenience and ease of use (e.g., "Simplify your projects with quick setup and reliable performance"). Both versions will be shown to a sample of hobbyists and small‑to‑medium manufacturers. Track click‑through and conversion (e.g., purchase intent) to assess which messaging drives engagement.
X1.sample: Target 2,000 hobbyists and small‑to‑medium manufacturers via Gühring’s existing B2B customer database, with a 1:1 split between Version A and Version B.
X1.measure: Conversion rate (purchases or purchase‑intent inquiries) for each version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Version A will generate a higher conversion rate than Version B because hobbyists and small manufacturers prioritize quality and precision for specific projects.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Version B will generate a higher conversion rate than Version A because hobbyists seek convenience and ease of use.

X1.decision_rule: If Version A’s conversion rate exceeds Version B’s by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing premium quality. If Version B’s conversion rate exceeds Version A’s by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with a consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, conduct further testing to refine messaging.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Gühring KG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial precision rotary cutting tools.

X1.name: Precision vs. Niche Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 self-identified hobbyists (DIY woodworkers, small metal fabricators) and 150 professional users (woodworkers, aerospace fabricators, CNC mill owners). Recruit via hobbyist forums and professional tool retailers.
X1.measure: Average WTP (in euros) for a Gühring tool described with either general hobbyist messaging (precision, reliability, durability) or niche messaging (precision woodwork, aerospace components). Secondary measure: stated primary purchase reason.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show higher average WTP for the general hobbyist message than for the niche message, and both will be above a €50 premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional users will show higher average WTP for the niche message than for the general hobbyist message, and both will be above a €50 premium.

X1.decision_rule: If hobbyist average WTP for general messaging exceeds niche messaging by at least €10, proceed with a differentiated hobbyist proposition. If professional users' average WTP for niche messaging exceeds general messaging by at least €10, proceed with a niche-focused proposition. If neither difference reaches the €10 threshold, do not expand.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Hobbyist vs Health‑Conscious Willingness‑to‑Pay Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) question.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobby brewers (self‑identified) and 250 health‑conscious consumers (self‑identified). Recruit via panel providers to ensure demographic balance.
X1.measure: Average WTP in euros for a small‑batch filling kit (e.g., 5‑liter) from Steinecker, measured on a 7‑point scale (1‑to‑7). Secondary measure: stated intent to purchase within six months.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobby brewers will show average WTP ≥ €200 and at least 10% will intend to purchase within six months.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Health‑conscious consumers will show average WTP ≥ €200 and at least 15% will intend to purchase within six months.

X1.decision_rule: If hobbyist average WTP ≥ €200 AND ≥ 10% intent → proceed to develop a differentiated consumer kit for hobby brewers (support T1). If health‑conscious average WTP ≥ €200 AND ≥ 15% intent → develop a differentiated consumer kit for health‑conscious consumers (support T2). If neither condition is met → no expansion justified.

revisions.reason: The simulated cleaning-offer test (SYN-KRONES-UPDATE) does not address consumer demand for a small-batch filling kit, so it does not affect T1. The theory remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay test (X1) to measure hobbyist demand for a small-batch filling kit. If the test meets the threshold (average WTP ≥ €200 and ≥10% intent), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer kit for hobby brewers. If not, explore other consumer use cases or no expansion. The test is the most direct way to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Hobby brewers (small-batch home brewers) who value easy, small-batch brewing.
final.value_proposition: A branded, easy-to-use small-batch filling kit that reduces the learning curve and perceived risk of home brewing.
final.next_action: Execute the 6‑week, €18,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 500 respondents (250 hobby brewers, 250 health‑conscious consumers) and apply the decision rule.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay and intent to purchase. The test is the primary source of validation.
would_change_if: If the test fails to meet the threshold (average WTP < €200 or <10% intent), the case for a consumer kit would weaken and we would reconsider no expansion or other use cases.

If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for eco‑friendly packaging (e.g., a willingness to pay premium for sustainable kits), T2 would become more likely and we would shift focus to that proposition.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. tool_result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Home Brewing Use Case Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a home brewing filling/packaging machine designed for small batches (e.g., Speidel Braumeister) and is asked to indicate whether they would purchase it for home use. Group B sees the same description and is asked to indicate whether they would purchase it for multiple pairs or as a medical necessity. Both groups are also asked about willingness to pay a premium.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 in Group A and 150 in Group B, recruited from regions with high craft brewery activity (e.g., U.S., Germany, UK).
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents in each group who select "Would purchase for home use" vs. "Would purchase for multiple pairs or as a medical necessity." Additionally, average willingness-to-pay premium (in euros) for Group A.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher percentage of respondents selecting "Would purchase for home use" than Group B, and the average willingness-to-pay premium will be higher for Group A.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher percentage of respondents selecting "Would purchase for multiple pairs or as a medical necessity" than Group A, and the average willingness-to-pay premium will be higher for Group B.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in the percentage of respondents selecting "Would purchase for home use" between Group A and Group B is at least 5 percentage points and the average willingness-to-pay premium for Group A is at least 20% higher than Group B, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home brewers. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points or the premium difference is less than 20%, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-KRONES-UPDATE) does not address home brewing demand, multiple pairs, or medical necessity; it tests cleaning burden, not consumer purchase drivers. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.value_proposition: Specialized filling and packaging machines designed for low-volume, home use, supported by accessories and consumables to extend the product's life.
final.next_action: Run the Home Brewing Use Case Preference Test (300 respondents, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for home use versus multiple pairs/medical necessity.
final.uncertainty: The actual size of the home brewing market and the relative importance of convenience versus multiple pairs/medical necessity are unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business.
