result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence does not conclusively support either theory; the consumer market is unproven and could be price-sensitive. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and price willingness under premium and trust positioning before any investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify U.I. Lapp GmbH investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial cable and connector offerings.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Search budget of 8 keyword searches.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that directly supports demand, willingness to pay, or a viable consumer route to market.
Must consider the company’s existing B2B core (machinery/plant engineering) and its broader B2B2C presence in food, logistics, energy, and mobility.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home networking, outdoor recreation, automotive aftermarket) with a new product or service model.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C presence by offering consumer‑focused versions of existing industrial products (e.g., lower‑cost cables, basic connectors) through retail or direct‑to-consumer channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current industrial machinery and plant engineering market, leveraging existing distribution and brand.
4) Partner with consumer brands or retailers to co‑brand or distribute consumer‑oriented versions of LAPP products, sharing marketing and distribution costs.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Networking Cable
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a LAPP consumer cable marketed for home networking, with either a premium positioning (industrial reliability, safety certification) or a trust positioning (proven industrial quality, safety). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home networking experience.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium positioning will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than trust positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trust positioning will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than premium positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If premium positioning yields a mean purchase intent of at least 5.5 and a mean price willingness to pay of at least €30, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If trust positioning yields a mean purchase intent of at least 5.5 and a mean price willingness to pay of at least €30, proceed to develop a trust-based consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Networking Cable
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a LAPP consumer cable marketed for home networking, with either a premium positioning (industrial reliability, safety certification) or a trust positioning (proven industrial quality, safety). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1-7) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home networking experience.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium positioning will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than trust positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trust positioning will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than premium positioning.

arguments.decision_rule: If premium positioning yields a mean purchase intent of at least 5.5 and a mean price willingness to pay of at least €30, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If trust positioning yields a mean purchase intent of at least 5.5 and a mean price willingness to pay of at least €30, proceed to develop a trust-based consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence does not conclusively support either theory; the consumer market is unproven and could be price-sensitive. Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and price willingness under premium and trust positioning before any investment.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify U.I. Lapp GmbH investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial cable and connector offerings.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Search budget of 8 keyword searches.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that directly supports demand, willingness to pay, or a viable consumer route to market.
Must consider the company’s existing B2B core (machinery/plant engineering) and its broader B2B2C presence in food, logistics, energy, and mobility.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home networking, outdoor recreation, automotive aftermarket) with a new product or service model.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C presence by offering consumer‑focused versions of existing industrial products (e.g., lower‑cost cables, basic connectors) through retail or direct‑to-consumer channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current industrial machinery and plant engineering market, leveraging existing distribution and brand.
4) Partner with consumer brands or retailers to co‑brand or distribute consumer‑oriented versions of LAPP products, sharing marketing and distribution costs.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Positioning
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two segments: (1) tech‑savvy, lifestyle‑oriented consumers (e.g., outdoor enthusiasts, e‑bike owners) and (2) price‑sensitive, functional‑focused consumers. Each segment views a product description of a consumer‑focused cable or connector for a specific use case (e.g., e‑bike charging cable). The description is presented with either a safety‑certified messaging frame (emphasizing reliability, certification, and industrial quality) or a lifestyle‑focused messaging frame (emphasizing community, quality, and brand alignment). Participants are then asked to indicate purchase intent (on a 7‑point scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 participants, 200 per segment, recruited via an online panel to match demographic characteristics of target consumers.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety‑certified messaging will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than lifestyle messaging among both segments.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Lifestyle‑focused messaging will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than safety‑certified messaging among both segments.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for safety‑certified messaging in the tech‑savvy segment is at least 1.5 points higher than for lifestyle messaging, and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed to develop a safety‑certified consumer proposition. If the average purchase intent for lifestyle messaging in the tech‑savvy segment is at least 1.5 points higher than for safety messaging, and the difference is statistically significant, proceed to develop a lifestyle‑focused consumer proposition. If neither segment shows a significant difference, do not expand into consumer products.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing food freshness and waste reduction; Group B sees a small‑business‑focused message emphasizing cost savings and freshness improvement. Both groups are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and intent to purchase.
X1.sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 30% higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B's WTP is at least 30% higher and the difference is statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, neither theory is supported.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE) does not show demand at the machine's price, nor that the household market is large enough, nor that a consumer business would sustain. It only tests whether running-cost messaging changes choice in a recruited group, so it does not address T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer positioned around food freshness and waste reduction, targeting serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts. Use the existing dealer network and online channels to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale messaging test (e.g., Group A vs. Group B) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale launch.
final.target_customer: Serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who already use vacuum-sealed food for sous vide and bulk food processing.
final.value_proposition: A consumer-friendly vacuum sealer that keeps food fresher longer, reduces waste, and is easy to use, leveraging MULTIVAC’s professional‑grade quality and existing distribution.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent under consumer‑focused versus small‑business‑focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: The household market is small and unproven; willingness to pay at the machine’s price is unknown. Small‑business demand is also uncertain and requires validation.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows Group B (small‑business focus) achieving at least 30% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group A, we would shift focus to T2 and develop a small‑business‑focused sealer.
If no test result meets the 30% threshold, we would reconsider the consumer proposition or explore other alternatives.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing food freshness and waste reduction; Group B sees a small‑business‑focused message emphasizing cost savings and freshness improvement. Both groups are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and intent to purchase.
arguments.sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels.
arguments.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 30% higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B's WTP is at least 30% higher and the difference is statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, neither theory is supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer positioned around food freshness and waste reduction, targeting serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts. Use the existing dealer network and online channels to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale messaging test (e.g., Group A vs. Group B) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale launch.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated result (SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE) does not show demand at the machine's price, nor that the household market is large enough, nor that a consumer business would sustain. It only tests whether running-cost messaging changes choice in a recruited group, so it does not address T1.
arguments.new_claim: none

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer positioned around food freshness and waste reduction, targeting serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts. Use the existing dealer network and online channels to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale messaging test (e.g., Group A vs. Group B) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale launch.
arguments.target_customer: Serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who already use vacuum-sealed food for sous vide and bulk food processing.
arguments.value_proposition: A consumer-friendly vacuum sealer that keeps food fresher longer, reduces waste, and is easy to use, leveraging MULTIVAC’s professional‑grade quality and existing distribution.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent under consumer‑focused versus small‑business‑focused messaging.
arguments.uncertainty: The household market is small and unproven; willingness to pay at the machine’s price is unknown. Small‑business demand is also uncertain and requires validation.
would_change_if: If the messaging test shows Group B (small‑business focus) achieving at least 30% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group A, we would shift focus to T2 and develop a small‑business‑focused sealer.
If no test result meets the 30% threshold, we would reconsider the consumer proposition or explore other alternatives.

tool_result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether MULTIVAC Sepp Haggenmüller SE & Co. KG should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current packaging and processing equipment, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.

Repeat purchase rate is high enough to offset marginal costs.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Sous Vide vs Bulk Storage
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two product pages for a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer: one emphasizing sous vide capabilities (professional-grade, liquid sealing, preset modes) and one emphasizing bulk food storage (large capacity, reusable bags, cost savings). Each page includes a price point and a "Buy Now" button. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely, 7‑Very likely) and state the primary reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for choosing the product (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the sous vide‑focused page will report purchase intent at least 15 points higher than those viewing the bulk‑storage page, and the primary reason will be "sous vide cooking" or "food preservation for sous vide."
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the bulk‑storage page will report purchase intent at least 15 points higher than those viewing the sous vide‑focused page, and the primary reason will be "bulk food storage" or "cost savings for meal prep."

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the sous vide and bulk‑storage pages is at least 15 points in favor of the sous vide page, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sous vide capabilities. If the difference is at least 15 points in favor of the bulk‑storage page, develop a proposition emphasizing bulk storage. If the difference is less than 15 points, conduct further market research before committing to a differentiated proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE does not address consumer motivation for convenience, cost savings, or sous vide/bulk food processing demand, nor does it provide evidence of premium pricing or repeat purchases. Therefore it does not affect the validity of T1.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Sous Vide vs Bulk Storage
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two product pages for a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer: one emphasizing sous vide capabilities (professional-grade, liquid sealing, preset modes) and one emphasizing bulk food storage (large capacity, reusable bags, cost savings). Each page includes a price point and a "Buy Now" button. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely, 7‑Very likely) and state the primary reason for choosing the product.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for choosing the product (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the sous vide‑focused page will report purchase intent at least 15 points higher than those viewing the bulk‑storage page, and the primary reason will be "sous vide cooking" or "food preservation for sous vide."
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the bulk‑storage page will report purchase intent at least 15 points higher than those viewing the sous vide‑focused page, and the primary reason will be "bulk food storage" or "cost savings for meal prep."

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the sous vide and bulk‑storage pages is at least 15 points in favor of the sous vide page, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sous vide capabilities. If the difference is at least 15 points in favor of the bulk‑storage page, develop a proposition emphasizing bulk storage. If the difference is less than 15 points, conduct further market research before committing to a differentiated proposition.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. X1.name: Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing professional-grade sous vide sealing and bulk food processing. Group B sees a small business-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing labor cost savings, faster packaging, and improved product freshness. Both groups see a neutral product description as a control. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels to ensure diversity in demographics and purchase intent.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s score is at least 1.5 points higher and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is supported and further evidence is needed.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing professional-grade sous vide sealing and bulk food processing. Group B sees a small business-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing labor cost savings, faster packaging, and improved product freshness. Both groups see a neutral product description as a control. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels to ensure diversity in demographics and purchase intent.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s score is at least 1.5 points higher and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is supported and further evidence is needed.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists, targeting small-scale producers who need reliable, affordable spinning equipment. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before scaling. Do not commit to small-scale producers yet; first test hobbyist willingness to pay a premium for a Rieter machine.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider Rieter’s existing B2B focus and its ownership of Barmag.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists or small-scale producers (e.g., compact spinning kits, DIY spinning machines).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new industrial features or services to existing short-staple spinning machines.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial spinning mills and after‑sales services.
4) License Barmag technology to third‑party consumer brands for spinning equipment.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hobbyists vs Small-Scale Producers
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to either a hobbyist or small-scale producer segment. Each segment sees a product description of a Rieter machine (differentiated for hobbyists and scalable for small-scale producers). Both segments see a price point (e.g., hobbyists pay 20% more, small-scale producers pay 15% more). Participants indicate their willingness to pay that price.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (self-identified) and 250 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruit via craft and small-farm forums.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents in each segment who indicate they would pay the specified premium price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 20% for a Rieter machine.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small-scale producers will show a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 15% for a machine that guarantees higher output and fewer breakdowns.

X1.decision_rule: If hobbyists' premium rate is at least 20% and small-scale producers' premium rate is at least 15%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists. If only one segment meets its threshold, do not invest in that segment. If neither meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: The simulated evidence (SYN-RIETER-UPDATE) does not provide real data on hobbyist willingness to pay a premium for Rieter machines; it is a hypothetical case-author construction. Therefore it does not affect the validity of T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists, targeting small-scale producers who need reliable, affordable spinning equipment. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before scaling. Do not commit to small-scale producers yet; first test hobbyist willingness to pay a premium for a Rieter machine.

arguments.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hobbyists vs Small-Scale Producers
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to either a hobbyist or small-scale producer segment. Each segment sees a product description of a Rieter machine (differentiated for hobbyists and scalable for small-scale producers). Both segments see a price point (e.g., hobbyists pay 20% more, small-scale producers pay 15% more). Participants indicate their willingness to pay that price.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (self-identified) and 250 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruit via craft and small-farm forums.
arguments.measure: Percentage of respondents in each segment who indicate they would pay the specified premium price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 20% for a Rieter machine.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small-scale producers will show a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 15% for a machine that guarantees higher output and fewer breakdowns.

arguments.decision_rule: If hobbyists' premium rate is at least 20% and small-scale producers' premium rate is at least 15%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists. If only one segment meets its threshold, do not invest in that segment. If neither meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for hobbyists, targeting small-scale producers who need reliable, affordable spinning equipment. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate demand before scaling. Do not commit to small-scale producers yet; first test hobbyist willingness to pay a premium for a Rieter machine.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer vs Industrial Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing affordability, compact design, and personal use; Group B sees an industrial-focused message emphasizing reliability, GRS certification, and B2B service support. Both groups view a product description of a compact spinning machine (identical spec).
X1.sample: 300 participants: 150 self-identified hobbyists/crafters and 150 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruited via craft and small-farm forums.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: satisfaction rating (1‑10).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B’s by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, proceed with a consumer proposition. If Group B’s intent exceeds Group A’s by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, proceed with an industrial proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand.

Therefore it does not contradict T1 and does not affect its status.

arguments.name: Consumer vs Industrial Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing affordability, compact design, and personal use; Group B sees an industrial-focused message emphasizing reliability, GRS certification, and B2B service support. Both groups view a product description of a compact spinning machine (identical spec).
arguments.sample: 300 participants: 150 self-identified hobbyists/crafters and 150 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruited via craft and small-farm forums.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: satisfaction rating (1‑10).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent exceeds Group B’s by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, proceed with a consumer proposition. If Group B’s intent exceeds Group A’s by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 20% higher, proceed with an industrial proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Rieter Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider Rieter’s existing B2B focus and its ownership of Barmag.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists or small-scale producers (e.g., compact spinning kits, DIY spinning machines).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new industrial features or services to existing short-staple spinning machines.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on industrial spinning mills and after‑sales services.
4) License Barmag technology to third‑party consumer brands for spinning equipment.

T1.claim: Individual crafters and small-scale producers will adopt Rieter spinning equipment if they perceive it as a reliable, sustainable way to produce handmade yarn, because they value quality and environmental responsibility.
T1.who_benefits: Crafters and small-scale yarn makers who already buy handmade yarn and are willing to invest in equipment they trust.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from buying ready-made yarn to producing their own yarn because they want to control quality, reduce waste, and align with sustainable practices, making the cost of the spinning machine a secondary consideration.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter captures value through premium pricing for high-quality equipment, loyalty to a brand associated with sustainability, and repeat purchases of additional accessories or services.
assumptions: Crafters are willing to pay more for equipment that reduces waste and is certified sustainable.
Sustainability is a primary driver for this segment, not just price or convenience.
Rieter can differentiate its consumer proposition from industrial offerings through design and branding.
There is a sufficient market of hobbyists and small producers willing to purchase.
predictions: If offered a differentiated consumer proposition, at least 30% of surveyed crafters will indicate intent to purchase a Rieter spinning machine within 12 months.
Sales of consumer kits will generate revenue comparable to existing B2B sales within the first year, provided pricing is appropriate for the segment.

X1.name: Consumer vs Small-Producer Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from two distinct groups: (1) hobbyists/crafters (n=200) and (2) small yarn producers (n=200). Each group sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sustainability, quality, and home use; (B) a small‑producer proposition emphasizing yield improvement, cost savings, and supply‑chain independence. Both descriptions include a price point and a call to action to purchase a Rieter spinning machine. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 hobbyists, 200 small producers) from the US and EU, recruited via online panels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product description.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hobbyists will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the consumer proposition than small producers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small producers will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the small‑producer proposition than hobbyists.

X1.decision_rule: If the consumer proposition achieves at least 30% purchase intent among hobbyists and at least 20% among small producers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the small‑producer proposition achieves at least 30% purchase intent among small producers and at least 20% among hobbyists, proceed to develop a small‑producer focused proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or small‑producer markets.

revisions.reason: The simulated onboarding offer test (SYN-RIETER-UPDATE) does not address purchase intent or willingness to pay for a Rieter consumer proposition; it tests a different mechanism (skill barrier vs. manual-onboarding). Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows crafters are interested in handmade yarn (survey) and Rieter already offers a small‑producer line (mini‑mill), but no source directly links purchase intent to sustainability or quality. Run the proposed messaging test to measure actual purchase intent before investing in a differentiated consumer proposition.
final.target_customer: Small yarn producers and hobbyists who already buy handmade yarn and are willing to invest in equipment they trust.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes sustainability, quality, and home use, leveraging Rieter’s existing brand and Barmag technology to offer a reliable, eco‑friendly spinning machine for individual crafters.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Small-Producer Messaging Test (400 participants, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for each product description.
final.uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market and whether they will pay a premium for sustainability are unknown. Small‑producer demand and willingness to pay for yield improvement are also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 20% among small producers or below 30% among hobbyists, we would reconsider expansion.
If new evidence shows strong demand for a small‑producer proposition, we would shift focus to that segment.
If a competitor launches a consumer‑focused spinning kit at a lower price, we would reassess the value proposition.

tool_result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kardex Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that Kardex can serve without major product redesign.
Any recommendation must consider Kardex’s existing B2B product portfolio and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners, renters, or small businesses for a specific use case (e.g., home office storage, hobby storage, or small retail).
2) Expand the B2B offering by adding new product features or services to existing systems (e.g., AI-driven inventory management, subscription services) without a new consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B warehouse, factory, and partner AutoStore cube storage systems.
4) Partner with or license Kardex technology to third‑party consumer brands for a specific use case, rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Cost Savings vs. Convenience
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a cost-saving proposition (e.g., 'Save EUR 200/year on storage costs with our compact vertical lift module') and a functional description of the product. Group B sees a convenience proposition (e.g., 'Easy access to stored items with remote control and app integration'). Both groups see the same product details and a call to pre-order or purchase.
X1.sample: 500 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: pre-order or purchase) and willingness to pay (maximum amount willing to pay).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B, because the cost-saving message directly addresses a measurable financial benefit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with modern living patterns and status.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B's, conclude T1 is more supported. If Group B's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A, conclude T2 is more supported. If the difference is below 15 percentage points, both theories remain equally supported and further testing is needed.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Cost Savings vs. Convenience
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a cost-saving proposition (e.g., 'Save EUR 200/year on storage costs with our compact vertical lift module') and a functional description of the product. Group B sees a convenience proposition (e.g., 'Easy access to stored items with remote control and app integration'). Both groups see the same product details and a call to pre-order or purchase.
arguments.sample: 500 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: pre-order or purchase) and willingness to pay (maximum amount willing to pay).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B, because the cost-saving message directly addresses a measurable financial benefit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with modern living patterns and status.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B's, conclude T1 is more supported. If Group B's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A, conclude T2 is more supported. If the difference is below 15 percentage points, both theories remain equally supported and further testing is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes measurable cost savings and space efficiency, targeting homeowners and small businesses. Use the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate whether a cost-saving message drives higher purchase intent than a convenience message. If the test confirms a 15-point or greater advantage for the cost-saving proposition, proceed with a consumer product line;

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated result (SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE) tests whether upfront cost changes choice among small workshop owners, not consumer demand. It does not address T1, which predicts cost savings drive purchase. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kardex Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that Kardex can serve without major product redesign.
Any recommendation must consider Kardex’s existing B2B product portfolio and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners, renters, or small businesses for a specific use case (e.g., home office storage, hobby storage, or small retail).
2) Expand the B2B offering by adding new product features or services to existing systems (e.g., AI-driven inventory management, subscription services) without a new consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B warehouse, factory, and partner AutoStore cube storage systems.
4) Partner with or license Kardex technology to third‑party consumer brands for a specific use case, rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from manual storage to automated systems when the payback period is short enough to justify the upfront cost, and when the system integrates with their existing workflow.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex captures value through higher-margin sales of integrated systems and recurring subscription revenue for maintenance and software updates.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Labor Cost vs Brand Prestige
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (labor cost savings) or Condition B (brand prestige). In Condition A, the offer emphasizes reduced labor costs and space efficiency. In Condition B, the offer emphasizes modern design, brand prestige, and ease of use. Both conditions include a price point and a purchase intent question.
arguments.sample: 500 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (250 per condition).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and willingness to pay (WTP) in a 7-point scale.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will generate at least 25% purchase intent and WTP at least 15% above Condition A.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.value_proposition: An integrated automated storage system that reduces labor costs, improves space efficiency, and offers a clear payback period, positioned as a cost-effective solution for individual storage needs.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Proposition Test (online survey with simulated purchase offer, 500 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000 budget) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under labor cost vs. brand prestige conditions.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Kardex is a trusted industrial brand with existing B2B reach, but no source directly addresses consumer demand, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay for home storage. The most credible source (Pio P100) is a B2B pay-per-pick model, not a consumer product. A limited pilot test (e.g., a small-scale willingness-to-pay survey) is needed to validate T1

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kardex Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that Kardex can serve without major product redesign.
Any recommendation must consider Kardex’s existing B2B product portfolio and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners, renters, or small businesses for a specific use case (e.g., home office storage, hobby storage, or small retail).
2) Expand the B2B offering by adding new product features or services to existing systems (e.g., AI-driven inventory management, subscription services) without a new consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B warehouse, factory, and partner AutoStore cube storage systems.
4) Partner with or license Kardex technology to third‑party consumer brands for a specific use case, rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small businesses gain better storage organization and lower maintenance costs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These buyers currently struggle with manual storage and high moving costs; automation reduces effort and expenses, making it attractive.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex can sell high-margin systems directly or through retail partners at premium prices justified by durability and reduced service needs.
assumptions: Consumers perceive Kardex as a trusted brand for industrial automation.
Price sensitivity is lower for one-time purchases of a premium system compared to recurring service contracts.
Retail distribution can reach individual buyers without major redesign.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners would indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above a comparable manual storage solution.
Pilot sales of a consumer-grade vertical lift module would show higher conversion than a B2B partner offering.
Repeat purchases or service contracts would be less common than with service contracts.

Kardex’s brand reputation for industrial reliability transfers to consumer perception.
predictions: Homeowners would indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above a comparable manual storage solution for a durable, long‑term system.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
