position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer expansion yet. The evidence base is limited and does not provide sufficient proof of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case. A small-scale test (e.g., the proposed Home Storage Preference Test) is recommended to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before any investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Kardex Holding AG investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B automated storage and retrieval systems.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that Kardex can serve without major product redesign.
Any recommendation must consider Kardex’s existing B2B product portfolio and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners, renters, or small businesses for a specific use case (e.g., home office storage, hobby storage, or small retail).
2) Expand the B2B offering by adding new product features or services to existing systems (e.g., AI-driven inventory management, subscription services) without a new consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B warehouse, factory, and partner AutoStore cube storage systems.
4) Partner with or license Kardex technology to third‑party consumer brands for a specific use case, rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case that Kardex can serve without major product redesign.
Any recommendation must consider Kardex’s existing B2B product portfolio and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners, renters, or small businesses for a specific use case (e.g., home office storage, hobby storage, or small retail).
2) Expand the B2B offering by adding new product features or services to existing systems (e.g., AI-driven inventory management, subscription services) without a new consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B warehouse, factory, and partner AutoStore cube storage systems.
4) Partner with or license Kardex technology to third‑party consumer brands for a specific use case, rather than creating a direct consumer brand.

arguments.name: Home Storage Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners and 250 small business owners recruited via a panel, balanced for age, income, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would purchase) or open-ended reason. 2) WTP: maximum price willing to pay for a Kardex consumer product. 3) Financial benefit perception: rating on a 1‑10 scale (e.g., property value increase, insurance cost reduction).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of homeowners will indicate purchase intent and WTP will be at least 20% above a comparable manual storage solution.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of homeowners will indicate purchase intent and WTP will be at least 15% above a comparable manual storage solution when the financial benefit is highlighted.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent among homeowners meets or exceeds the respective thresholds (30% for T1 and 25% for T2) AND WTP for the consumer product is at least 20% above a comparable manual storage solution, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a consumer expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer expansion yet. The evidence base is limited and does not provide sufficient proof of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a clear use case. A small-scale test (e.g., the proposed Home Storage Preference Test) is recommended to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before any investment.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

arguments.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.
arguments.sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. tool_result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: DIY Messaging Test: Professional vs Convenience Framing
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Professional Condition (highlighting professional-grade performance, reliability, and use by contractors) or Convenience Condition (highlighting easy application, minimal skill required, and time savings). After viewing the product description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a premium over a generic alternative.
X1.sample: Proposed sample: 1,200 homeowners (600 per condition) from a panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience. Recruitment cost: €2,000.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (Professional Condition vs Convenience Condition). Secondary measure: premium willingness to pay (difference in price premium indicated).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Professional Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Convenience Condition will yield higher average purchase intent and premium willingness to pay than Professional Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Professional Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Convenience Condition (i.e., Professional ≥ 5.5 and Convenience ≤ 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. position.recommendation: Run the proposed Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test (X1) to empirically compare household adoption of a digital refund app versus a sensor-based bag‑drop system. The test will determine whether the stated convenience of the app (T1) translates into actual demand, and whether the cost‑saving mechanism (T2) is viable for retailers. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels; otherwise, proceed.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to capture value for individual consumers.
Any recommendation must consider TOMRA’s existing B2B customers and current product portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition targeting individual households (e.g., home recycling for single‑use containers).
2) Expand B2B offerings by targeting new segments such as small retailers, food processors, or mining companies with additional sorting or recycling solutions.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets without new consumer initiatives.
4) License TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting technology to third‑party consumer brands for integrated recycling solutions.

T1.claim: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s consumer app provides real, immediate digital refunds rather than relying on traditional redemption centers or bag‑drop systems.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers gain convenience and instant cash; TOMRA captures recurring revenue through digital refunds and may increase collection volumes.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently must travel to redemption centers or bag‑drop points for refunds; the app eliminates that friction and makes recycling feel rewarding through digital payout.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA earns per‑transaction fees or subscription fees from digital refunds, and can use data on container types to improve sorting efficiency and lower costs.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a small fee for digital refunds.
TOMRA can integrate digital refund processing into its existing systems without significant hardware changes.
Regulatory requirements allow digital payout of refunds in target markets.
predictions: A pilot offering the app in a single market will achieve at least 5% of target households downloading the app within 3 months.
Average refund value will be at least €0.50, with a conversion rate of at least 10% of collected containers processed through the app.
T1.first_claim: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s consumer app provides real, immediate digital refunds rather than relying on traditional redemption centers or bag‑drop systems.

T2.claim: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting machines reduce the cost of recycling for retailers and food processors, making it cheaper to collect and process containers than current methods.
T2.who_benefits: Retailers and food processors gain lower recycling costs and improved supply chain efficiency; TOMRA captures value through higher volume sales of sorting machines and potential licensing of its sensor technology.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Current recycling methods (e.g., bag drops, redemption centers) are expensive for retailers and food processors; sensor‑based sorting lowers labor and material costs, making recycling more profitable and attractive.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA earns per‑unit sales of sorting machines and can license its sensor technology to other retailers, generating recurring revenue and market expansion.
assumptions: Retailers and food processors are willing to invest in sensor‑based sorting if it reduces their recycling costs.
TOMRA can scale its sensor technology to meet the needs of multiple retailers and food processors.
Regulatory requirements do not prohibit the use of sensor‑based sorting in the target markets.
predictions: A pilot deployment of sensor‑based sorting in a single retail or food‑processing facility will achieve at least 15% reduction in recycling costs compared to current methods within 6 months.
At least 20% of target retailers or food processors will express interest in purchasing the sensor‑based sorting system within 12 months.
T2.first_claim: Households will adopt home recycling for single‑use containers if TOMRA’s sensor‑based sorting machines reduce the cost of recycling for retailers and food processors, making it cheaper to collect and process containers than current methods.

X1.name: Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test
X1.method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct markets (e.g., NSW, Australia) with identical consumer messaging but different mechanisms: in Market A, households download the myTOMRA app and collect containers via the app; in Market B, households use a sensor‑based bag‑drop system (e.g., C&C Consolidated Holdings). Track app downloads, digital refund uptake, and container return rates.
X1.sample: 10,000 households per market, recruited via social media and local partnerships, balanced for age, income, and recycling behavior.
X1.measure: 1) App downloads and active users within 3 months. 2) Average refund value per household (digital payout). 3) Container return rate (percentage of collected containers processed through the app vs. bag drop).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Market A will achieve at least 5% app downloads and an average refund value of €0.50, with a return rate of at least 10% of collected containers processed through the app.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Market B will achieve at least 15% reduction in recycling costs for the participating retailer or food processor, and at least 20% of target retailers will express interest in purchasing the sensor‑based sorting system within 12 months.

X1.decision_rule: If Market A meets both the 5% download threshold and the 10% return rate threshold, proceed to develop a consumer app proposition. If Market B meets the 15% cost‑reduction threshold and the 20% interest threshold, invest in a sensor‑based sorting pilot for retailers. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE) does not address digital refund mechanisms or household adoption of a consumer app; it tests a different mechanism (doorstep vs store drop-off) and does not provide evidence for or against T1. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed Digital vs Sensor Pilot Test (X1) to empirically compare household adoption of a digital refund app versus a sensor-based bag‑drop system. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or B2B channels; otherwise, proceed.
final.target_customer: Individual households in markets where deposit return systems are already in place (e.g., NSW, Australia, EU).
final.value_proposition: A consumer app that provides real, immediate digital refunds for returned containers, eliminating the need to visit redemption centers or bag‑drop points.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week pilot in two markets, tracking app downloads, digital refund uptake, and container return rates against the proposed thresholds.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on household willingness to pay for digital refunds and on the cost‑saving impact of sensor‑based sorting for retailers.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows at least 5% app downloads and a 10% return rate, T1 would become more credible and would justify developing a consumer app proposition.
If the pilot shows at least 15% cost reduction for retailers and 20% interest in purchasing sensor‑based sorting, T2 would become more credible and would justify investing in a sensor pilot.
If neither threshold is met, both theories would be weakened and the recommendation would shift to no expansion.

arguments.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a consumer-facing deposit return system if it offers a convenient, digital refund mechanism and a clear path to return containers, because convenience and digital payout reduce the effort and friction of the return process.
arguments.who_benefits: Households that need to return beverage containers and receive immediate digital refunds.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently face the hassle of visiting a physical return point or redemption center. A digital app that allows returns and refunds online removes this friction, making recycling more convenient and attractive.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA can capture value by selling the app as a subscription or one-time purchase, earning recurring revenue from refunds and potentially charging for premium features like loyalty points or bundled recycling services.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a digital refund service.
The digital platform can be integrated with existing deposit return infrastructure without major hardware changes.
Regulatory requirements allow digital payout of refunds.
predictions: In a test market, households using the digital app will return containers at a higher rate than those using only physical return points.

arguments.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA can capture value by partnering with retailers to offer reward points or discounts, and by selling a subscription-based loyalty platform that earns revenue from reward redemptions.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a TOMRA consumer proposition because they seek convenience and financial incentives (e.g., digital refunds), and the app offers a fun, low‑barrier way to recycle, leading to higher participation rates.
T1.who_benefits: Individual households with single‑use containers seeking easy recycling and refund.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently face multiple recycling trips and limited refund methods; the app simplifies the process and provides immediate digital refund, reducing friction and increasing willingness to recycle.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through subscription fees or a share of refund payouts to users, leveraging its existing myTOMRA platform to reach consumers and monetize digital refunds.
assumptions: Consumers value convenience and financial incentives more than traditional drop‑off methods.
The app can reach a sufficient user base to generate meaningful refund payouts.
TOMRA can afford the development and marketing cost of a consumer app within the €20,000 budget.
predictions: A pilot app with a digital refund feature will achieve at least 5,000 monthly active users within 12 weeks.
Users will return containers at a rate 1.5‑times higher than standard drop‑off methods.
TOMRA will generate at least €50,000 in refund payouts during the pilot.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers are motivated by the desire to make a positive environmental impact; the app offers real-time tracking and a community element that makes recycling feel personal and rewarding.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through brand association with sustainability, potential partnerships with environmental organizations, and optional premium features that enhance the user experience.
assumptions: Environmental awareness is a significant driver for consumer recycling behavior.
Transparency and community features increase perceived impact and engagement.
TOMRA can leverage its existing reputation in recycling to build trust with eco-conscious consumers.
predictions: A pilot app with environmental tracking and community features will achieve at least 3,000 monthly active users within 12 weeks.
Users will report higher satisfaction and intent to continue recycling compared to a control group without these features.
TOMRA will generate at least €30,000 in brand-related revenue during the pilot.

X1.name: Digital Refund vs Environmental Tracking Pilot
X1.method: Run a 12‑week pilot with two parallel groups of 2,000 individuals recruited via social media. Group A receives a TOMRA consumer app with a digital refund feature and a convenience message. Group B receives the same app but with environmental tracking and community features. Both groups are offered a small refund credit (e.g., €5) for recycling 10 containers. Track monthly active users and refund payout.
X1.sample: 4,000 individuals (2,000 per group) recruited in the UK and Germany, targeting households with single‑use containers.
X1.measure: Monthly active users of the app and refund payout (total refund value paid out).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will achieve at least 5,000 monthly active users and generate at least €50,000 in refund payouts.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will achieve at least 3,000 monthly active users and generate at least €30,000 in refund payouts.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s refund payout exceeds Group B’s by ≥ €20,000, proceed with a consumer proposition focused on digital refunds. If Group B’s refund payout exceeds Group A’s by ≥ €20,000, reconsider the environmental tracking approach. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that offers a digital refund mechanism tied to shopping habits, as it aligns with evidence that consumers return containers at retail locations and value convenience. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to capture value for individual consumers.

alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer proposition targeting individual households (e.g., home recycling for single‑use containers).

T1.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a convenient, digital refund mechanism that ties recycling to their shopping habits, because convenience and immediate financial reward reduce the perceived effort and friction of recycling.
T1.who_benefits: Households that currently return containers at retail locations but lack a digital payout option.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a manual, location-specific return process to a digital app that allows refunds at any time, making recycling feel less like a chore and more like a reward.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through app revenue, subscription fees, and potential partnerships with retailers to promote the service.
assumptions: Consumers value immediate financial return over other recycling incentives.
Retailers will partner to integrate the app into their existing return systems.
The digital platform can be scaled without significant additional hardware costs.
predictions: In a test market, households using the digital app will return containers at a rate at least 20% higher than those using a traditional manual system.
Surveyed users will report that the digital refund is the primary reason for returning containers.
Retailers will report increased foot traffic or sales at participating locations.
T1.first_claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a convenient, digital refund mechanism that ties recycling to their shopping habits, because convenience and immediate financial reward reduce the perceived effort and friction of recycling.

T2.claim: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it offers a tangible reward (e.g., cash, discounts, or loyalty points) for recycling, because the immediate tangible benefit creates a stronger incentive than a digital refund alone.
T2.who_benefits: Households that currently return containers but do not receive any financial return.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from a location-specific return process to a reward-based system because the tangible benefit provides a clear, measurable outcome that can be tracked and redeemed.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA captures value through reward program revenue, partner retailer incentives, and potential data monetization of recycling behavior.
assumptions: Consumers are motivated by immediate financial or non-financial rewards rather than convenience alone.
Retailers will be willing to allocate resources to reward programs.
The reward mechanism can be integrated without requiring new hardware or significant infrastructure changes.
predictions: In a test market, households receiving a reward will return containers at a rate at least 15% higher than those receiving only a digital refund.
Surveyed users will cite the reward as the primary reason for returning containers.
Retailers will report increased foot traffic or sales at locations offering the reward program.

X1.name: Digital Refund vs Reward Test
X1.method: Randomized controlled trial with two arms: Arm A receives a digital refund via a mobile app; Arm B receives a tangible reward (e.g., a discount or loyalty point) for recycling. Participants are recruited from a retail location and asked to return beverage containers. The test runs for 4 weeks, with participants in each arm receiving a separate message about the reward mechanism.
X1.sample: 200 households (100 per arm) recruited from a single retail location in a mid-sized city, ensuring diversity in age, gender, and income.
X1.measure: Primary measure: number of containers returned per participant per week. Secondary measures: self-reported reason for returning (convenience vs reward) and willingness to pay a small fee for the reward.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show at least 20% higher return rates than Arm B, and participants will cite convenience as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show at least 15% higher return rates than Arm A, and participants will cite the reward as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If Arm A return rate exceeds Arm B by at least 20 percentage points, conclude T1 is supported. If Arm B return rate exceeds Arm A by at least 15 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.

arguments.name: Digital Refund vs Reward Test
arguments.method: Randomized controlled trial with two arms: Arm A receives a digital refund via a mobile app; Arm B receives a tangible reward (e.g., a discount or loyalty point) for recycling. Participants are recruited from a retail location and asked to return beverage containers. The test runs for 4 weeks, with participants in each arm receiving a separate message about the reward mechanism.
arguments.sample: 200 households (100 per arm) recruited from a single retail location in a mid-sized city, ensuring diversity in age, gender, and income.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: number of containers returned per participant per week. Secondary measures: self-reported reason for returning (convenience vs reward) and willingness to pay a small fee for the reward.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show at least 20% higher return rates than Arm B, and participants will cite convenience as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show at least 15% higher return rates than Arm A, and participants will cite the reward as the primary reason.

arguments.decision_rule: If Arm A return rate exceeds Arm B by at least 20 percentage points, conclude T1 is supported. If Arm B return rate exceeds Arm A by at least 15 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Brembo N.V. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current brake systems and aftermarket replacement parts, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to pay and a viable business model for Brembo.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., performance brake kits for hobbyists, racing enthusiasts, or custom builds).
2) Expand the aftermarket by offering premium replacement parts or service contracts for individual consumers.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B brake systems and aftermarket parts without new consumer offerings.

X1.name: Digital Messaging Test for Performance Brake Kit
X1.method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign with two versions: Version A (performance-focused) and Version B (lifestyle-focused). Both ads feature a Brembo brake kit at a premium price (e.g., €1,200). Version A emphasizes heritage, performance, and sporty aesthetics; Version B emphasizes lifestyle, status, and the Brembo lifestyle collection. Track clicks, conversions, and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: Estimated 5,000 individual buyers in the UK and Germany who have shown interest in performance upgrades (e.g., visited a performance car forum or purchased an upgrade kit in the past 12 months).
X1.measure: Conversion rate (percentage of visitors who click the buy button) and average willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Version A will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version B, because performance-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to performance messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Version B will generate a higher conversion rate and higher average willingness to pay than Version A, because lifestyle-oriented buyers are more likely to respond to status and brand messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If Version A conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a performance-focused consumer proposition. If Version B conversion rate >= 5% and average willingness to pay >= €1,200, proceed with a lifestyle-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer offerings.

There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. tool_result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

frame.objective: Determine whether Brembo N.V. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current brake systems and aftermarket replacement parts, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Evidence must demonstrate consumer willingness to pay and a viable business model for Brembo.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., performance brake kits for hobbyists, racing enthusiasts, or custom builds).

3) No expansion: continue focusing on B2B brake systems and aftermarket parts without new consumer offerings.

If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer offerings.

X1.name: Premium vs Community Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees premium messaging emphasizing precision, quality, and professional-grade performance. Group B sees community messaging emphasizing collaboration, shared learning, and a makerspace experience. Both groups view a mock Biesse desktop CNC machine description and are asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (20% above baseline price) and likelihood to purchase.
X1.sample: 300 individual woodworkers and hobbyists recruited via online panels, balanced across the two groups (150 per group).
X1.measure: Willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more) and purchase intent (binary: would purchase).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s willingness to pay premium exceeds Group B by at least 5 percentage points, adopt T1. If Group B’s willingness to pay premium exceeds Group A by at least 5 percentage points, adopt T2. If the difference is ≥ 5 percentage points, proceed with the corresponding differentiated proposition. If the difference is ≤ 5 percentage points, consider no expansion.

revisions.reason: The simulated source SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE does not address individual hobbyists or their willingness to pay a premium for Biesse machines; it tests a narrow mechanism (simplified software vs standard software) among a recruited group. Therefore it does not affect T1, which posits that individual woodworkers will purchase Biesse machines because they value precision, quality, and professional-grade performance.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes precision, quality, and professional-grade performance, targeting individual woodworkers and hobbyists who value high-end results. Use premium pricing and marketing to capture higher margins and brand credibility. Conduct a small-scale test (e.g., willingness-to-pay survey) to validate demand before scaling.
final.target_customer: Individual woodworkers and hobbyists who purchase CNC machines for personal projects and value accuracy, reliability, and professional-grade performance.
final.value_proposition: A premium Biesse machine that delivers industrial-grade precision, quality, and reliability, positioned as the tool for serious woodworkers who need to produce high-quality, professional-grade results.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Premium vs Community Messaging Test (or a similar willingness-to-pay survey) to measure actual demand for premium positioning versus community messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the individual hobbyist market and their willingness to pay a premium for Biesse machines is uncertain. The overall weak market demand for wood processing (as indicated by the Q3 2026 report) could affect demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay premium is below 5 percentage points, indicating insufficient demand, the recommendation would shift to no expansion or a lower-priced consumer proposition.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.sample: 300 participants: 150 from hobbyist/DIY forums and 150 from makerspace/DIY communities, balanced across regions with varying hobbyist activity.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (7-point scale) for each messaging condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Performance messaging will generate higher average WTP and purchase intent than community messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Community messaging will generate higher average WTP and purchase intent than performance messaging.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Hobbyist Preference Test: Precision vs. Accessibility
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios for a desktop CNC machine. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Precision Group (professional-grade, high-accuracy machine) and Accessibility Group (easy-to-use, small-project machine). Each group sees a product description and a price point, and is asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 300 participants: 150 per group, recruited from DIY and makerspace communities via social media and forums.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated primary purchase driver (precision vs. ease of use).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Precision Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Accessibility Group, indicating demand for professional-grade performance.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Accessibility Group will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Precision Group, indicating demand for ease of use and small projects.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent of the Precision Group is at least 10 points higher than the Accessibility Group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on precision and professional-grade performance. result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of health benefits and the availability of AI-powered, smart home integration make home automation robots an attractive purchase for personal use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Nabtesco would sell differentiated home-use products directly to consumers, leveraging its existing brand reputation and ability to design assistive devices, and could charge higher prices than standard consumer electronics.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for health and convenience features.
Nabtesco can adapt its existing precision reduction gears and control technology for small, affordable home units.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

arguments.objective: Determine whether Nabtesco Corporation should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home automation, outdoor recreation, or personal health) sold directly to individual consumers.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Rehabilitation vs Lifestyle Positioning
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with interest in home automation and assistive devices. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Medical necessity positioning (emphasizing therapeutic benefits, rehabilitation, and family support) or (B) Lifestyle positioning (emphasizing design, comfort, and home aesthetics). After viewing a product description and price, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 homeowners (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the medical necessity condition compared to lifestyle condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the lifestyle condition compared to medical necessity condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for medical necessity condition is at least 10 points higher than for lifestyle condition (i.e., medical necessity ≥ lifestyle + 10), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for medical necessity. If the difference is less than 10 points, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

arguments.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Rehabilitation vs Lifestyle Positioning
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with interest in home automation and assistive devices. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Medical necessity positioning (emphasizing therapeutic benefits, rehabilitation, and family support) or (B) Lifestyle positioning (emphasizing design, comfort, and home aesthetics). After viewing a product description and price, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 400 homeowners (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the medical necessity condition compared to lifestyle condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the lifestyle condition compared to medical necessity condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for medical necessity condition is at least 10 points higher than for lifestyle condition (i.e., medical necessity ≥ lifestyle + 10), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for medical necessity. If the difference is less than 10 points, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated result (SYN-NABTESCO-UPDATE) does not address homeowner purchase motivations; it tests a narrow mechanism (safety assurance vs specification) in a recruited group. Therefore it does not affect T1, which posits medical necessity drives purchase.

tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
